title: Parts and Recreation
prompt: Our client is an Automotive Original Equipment Manufacturer or OEM. They have approached you to build a growth strategy. Please go ahead.

notes.title: Keep In Mind
items: Grow parts per car, not volume
Raise value instead of cutting price

framework:
Candidate: Thank you. Before I structure my approach, I'd like to ask a few clarifying questions. To confirm my understanding, an Original Equipment Manufacturer is a company that produces the actual vehicles along with the parts that go into them. Is that the right way to think about our client?
Interviewer: That's correct.
Candidate: I'd also like to know which part of the business we are focusing on. Is it the vehicle manufacturing business as a whole, or one specific division?
Interviewer: Good question. The client is the spare parts division of an automobile company. That is who has come to us.
Candidate: Understood. For spare parts, I see two broad ways the business can operate. First, a product channel, where we sell spare parts to retailers who then sell them onward. Second, a service channel, where we fit and service the spare parts ourselves for the customer. Do we run both of these?
Interviewer: Yes, that's a good observation. We have both a product channel and a service channel.
Candidate: One more point on the product itself. Can our spare parts be used only in the cars that our own company manufactures, or can they also be fitted in other companies' cars?
Interviewer: They can only be used on our own cars.
Candidate: That's helpful. Finally, I'd like to understand the goal. Are we targeting revenue growth (top line) or profit growth (bottom line), and what is the target and the time frame?
Interviewer: We are looking at revenue growth (top line). The client wants to double its revenue over the next 2 to 3 years.
Candidate: Got it. To structure this, growth can come from two directions: organic growth and inorganic growth. For a spare parts business, I don't think inorganic growth makes much sense. Since our parts can only be used on our own cars, acquiring another company would add limited value and would take a lot of time to merge and fine tune into our operations. So I'd set inorganic growth aside and focus on organic growth. Does that sound fair?
Interviewer: Yes, that sounds fair.
Candidate: For organic growth, I'd break revenue into three levers:
Organic Revenue = Number of Cars × Spare Parts per Car × Price per Spare Part
One quick check before I go deeper: should we also look at increasing the number of cars sold, since more cars on the road directly increases the demand for spare parts?
Interviewer: That's a good observation, but the client is only the spare parts division. So let's focus there.
Candidate: Understood. I'll set the number of cars aside and focus on increasing the number of spare parts sold per car and the price per part. To go deeper, I'd look at our two routes to market separately: the product channel and the service channel.
Interviewer: Let's start with the service channel.
Candidate: Sure. In the service channel, customers come to us directly to get their cars serviced, and we fit our own spare parts during that service. I'd split this channel into two routes: a Direct-to-Consumer route, or D2C, where we deal with the end customer, and a Business-to-Business route, or B2B, where we work with other businesses. Let me start with the Direct-to-Consumer route. I'd think about it in two stages: before the customer buys the car, and after they own it. Before the purchase, there are two opportunities. First, mandatory fitments that are built into the car automatically, for example a spare tyre. At the moment of buying the car, an extra 4,000 to 5,000 rupees for these fitments feels small to the customer, so they rarely object. Second, optional add-ons that the customer can choose to include.
Interviewer: And after the purchase?
Candidate: After the purchase, I'd offer one free service or one free repair along with the car. Customers usually hesitate to visit the official service centre at first. A free first service brings them in, lets them experience the quality of our work, and makes them far more likely to return to us when a real issue comes up later.
Interviewer: What is the biggest pain point that would push a customer towards a local retailer instead of us?
Candidate: The biggest pain point is price sensitivity. Local retailers are usually cheaper.
Interviewer: So how would you counter that price sensitivity?
Candidate: We can't undercut retailers. Our genuine parts and better service cost more. Instead, I'd raise the value proposition by bundling servicing costs into the customer's existing car EMI. For example, our 10,000 rupee service versus a local retailer's 5,000 rupees feels expensive upfront. But spread across the EMI, it's only an extra hundred rupees per month, making our higher quality option far more affordable.
Interviewer: Alright. Let's move to the Business-to-Business route within the service channel.
Candidate: In the Business-to-Business route, I'd set up a milestone-based incentive program. Partners who hit volume targets earn better terms, and top performers become authorized partners. This creates a win-win: customers trust the authorized badge, retailers get more business from our brand's customers, and we drive more sales through the partner network.
Interviewer: Good. Can you summarise the case for me?
Candidate: Certainly. Our client is the spare parts division of an automotive OEM that wants to double its revenue in 2 to 3 years. We focused on organic growth and set inorganic growth aside, since our parts only fit our own cars. Within organic growth, we concentrated on selling more spare parts through two channels. In the service channel, on the Direct-to-Consumer side, we capture value before purchase through mandatory fitments and optional add-ons, and after purchase through a free first service that builds trust, supported by EMI bundling to overcome price sensitivity. On the Business-to-Business side, we use a milestone based incentive and authorized partner program to grow sales through our partner network.
Interviewer: That's a clear summary. We can close the case here.
